e: Borrowed from Classical Persian سَحَرِی (saharī), with the variants sahri and sehri by way of Hindustani سَحْری (sahrī) / सहरी (sahrī), ultimately from Arabic سَحَر (saḥar, “dawn”).
From a Tupian language in the area of Bahia, Brazil. A variant form or cognate of sagoin.

e: From Hindustani صاحب / साहिब (sāhib, “lord”), from Classical Persian صاحب (sāhib), from Arabic صَاحِب (ṣāḥib, “companion”).
q: One day when the Man's Wife and the Tertium Quid had just arrived in the Cemetery, they saw some coolies breaking ground. They had marked out a full-size grave, and the Tertium Quid asked them whether any Sahib was sick. They said that they did not know; but it was an order that they should dig a Sahib's grave.
